When disabled, it returns whatever the provider-specific refresh function returns (e.g. for googlecalendar `myGoogleAuth.refreshToken(...)` returns `{ res: { data: {...} } }`, for hubspot it returns a HubspotToken, etc.). Downstream callers were written assuming the non-sync shape. With sharing enabled the googlecalendar code at `packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:94` does `const token = res?.data;` on a Response, then `token.access_token` throws TypeError. hubspot (`hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts:192`), office365calendar (`office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` after `parseRefreshTokenResponse`), office365video (`office365video/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts:77`), zohocrm (`zohocrm/lib/CalendarService.ts:204`), zoho-bigin (`zoho-bigin/lib/CalendarService.ts:85`), webex (`webex/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts:62`) and zoomvideo (`zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts:79`) all break the same way. The function must return a normalized token object (parsed from the sync JSON plus token shape) and propagate provider-specific data on the non-sync branch, or each integration needs its own dispatcher.

findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema Zod schema does not validate what the comments claim
findings.body: Computed property keys in object literals evaluate to fixed strings at runtime: `[z.string().toString()]` yields the literal string `"ZodString"` (the ZodType's toString), not 'any string key'. The resulting schema is therefore `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), ZodString: z.number(), ZodOptional: z.unknown().optional() })`. Real token responses from the self-hoster's sync endpoint don't include a `ZodString` number field, so `safeParse` will fail (the required `ZodString` number is missing), throwing "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". The comments claim it allows any number property as expiry and any other properties, but neither is true. The correct way to express that is `.catchall(z.unknown())` on the object, or leaving the schema as-is and not adding the placeholder keys.

findings.title: Placeholder string 'refresh_token' written into credential.key.refresh_token
findings.body: When the parsed response has no `refresh_token`, the code sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"` (a literal placeholder). That string is then persisted into `credential.key.refresh_token` via the callers (e.g. googlecalendar `CalendarService.ts` writes `key` into the DB, office365calendar writes the merged `o365AuthCredentials`, etc.). On the next refresh cycle the placeholder will be used as the actual `refresh_token` against Google/Microsoft/etc. and will be rejected as invalid_grant, permanently breaking the credential. If the sync endpoint does not return a `refresh_token`, refresh tokens must be left undefined and the credential marked invalid instead of being silently corrupted.

findings.title: Webhook endpoint allows writing credentials for arbitrary user IDs with a single shared secret
findings.body: The endpoint authenticates the caller only with a single shared header secret (lines 24-29). Once that secret is known (it is shared by every Cal.com deployment enabling this feature and there is no per-tenant signing), any caller can POST `{userId: <int>, appSlug, keys}` and overwrite that user's credentials. `userId` is a sequential integer from the users table, so attackers can iterate. There is no per-user HMAC, no per-deployment signing key bound to the user, and no proof that the caller is authorized to manage that specific user's third-party account. Concretely this lets one compromised self-host instance push attacker-controlled OAuth tokens (which can include an `access_token` issued to the attacker's account on Google/Microsoft/Zoom/etc.) into any user's Cal.com account, which the app will then use to read/insert calendar events and create meetings on behalf of the victim. Also note the header comparison `req.headers[name] !== secret` is non-constant-time and will throw/always-fail if the header is sent twice (Next.js parses duplicate headers as an array).

findings.title: SalesforceCalendarService.refreshes access token on every getClient() call
findings.body: Lines 75-100 unconditionally POST to Salesforce's token endpoint inside `getClient`, then overwrite `credential.key` in the database, even when the existing access token is still valid. `getClient` is called once per service instance (line 57), so a service that is held across many operations will refresh exactly once per construction - but more importantly, every API operation that constructs a new `SalesforceCalendarService` (which is the typical usage pattern in this repo, see e.g. how other CalendarService implementations are instantiated per-call) hits Salesforce for a token refresh whether or not refresh is required. This both wastes a refresh_token use (Salesforce will eventually return `invalid_grant` once the refresh token rotates out) and can trip rate limits. Refresh should be gated on token expiry, mirroring the other integrations (`isExpired` checks before calling refresh).

findings.title: fetch() to sync endpoint has no Content-Type header and no auth
findings.body: The body is `new URLSearchParams({...})` but no `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded` header is set, so the receiving server is not guaranteed to parse the body as a form (it will see an empty body in many frameworks, and `calcomUserId`/`appSlug` will be undefined server-side, making every refresh call effectively a no-op). Additionally, there is no authentication on this outbound call: the sync endpoint cannot distinguish a request coming from this Cal.com instance from any other HTTP client that knows the URL. The endpoint should at minimum require a shared secret / signature header that the self-hoster validates.

findings.title: Sync endpoint HTTP errors are not detected; raw Response is returned
findings.body: The function returns the `Response` object unconditionally (line 15) without checking `response.ok`. If the self-hoster's sync endpoint returns 401/403/429/500, the raw error response body is handed to downstream code as if it were a successful token response, then parsed with the (already broken) `minimumTokenResponseSchema` and discarded, leaving the credential unchanged on disk with no error logged. The caller has no way to know refresh failed. A `if (!response.ok) throw new Error(...)` is required, and the function should surface token refresh failures.

findings.title: findFirst + create/update on credentials is not atomic (race condition / duplicate rows)
findings.body: Lines 62-90 do a `findFirst` followed by either `update` or `create` on `prisma.credential` based on whether a row was found. There is no transaction or unique constraint check; if two webhook calls for the same (userId, appId) race (e.g. the self-hoster retries, or a user reinstalls while a webhook is in flight), both can observe no existing row and both `create`, producing two credential rows for the same user/app. Subsequent refresh/lookup code in this repo commonly uses `findFirst` for these (e.g. office365video callback line 79 does `findMany` and deletes duplicates by hand, but the webhook path does not), which means the duplicate row will be silently picked up by whichever path queries first and the other becomes dead weight (or causes the wrong row to be updated). The (userId, appId) pair needs a unique constraint or the write needs to use an upsert/transaction.

findings.title: Decryption failure and bad payload not handled
findings.body: `symmetricDecrypt` will throw if the encrypted blob is malformed or the key is wrong, and `JSON.parse` will throw if the decrypted plaintext is not valid JSON. Neither is caught, so the handler returns a 500 with the stack trace leaking to the caller instead of a 4xx with a clear message. Also, after a successful decrypt+parse, `keys` is `unknown` (since it is `JSON.parse(...)`); it is written to `credential.key` without any schema check (no zod, no type guard), so any JSON object - including something that isn't a valid OAuth token shape - will be persisted. At minimum the handler should validate `keys` is an object with the fields the downstream app actually expects, and wrap the decrypt+parse in try/catch returning 400.
